output.title: Acceptance walkthroughs as a design constraint
output.body:
If you are automating work in a small business, acceptance walkthroughs should be a design constraint, not an afterthought. I mean a simple owner check before AI output touches money, a customer promise, or any system that would be annoying to unwind later. That keeps the workflow honest: the system assists decisions, while the person who owns the business keeps the final say.

For a 1–10-person team, the useful question is not “Can AI do this?” but “Where do I want a human pause?” In our own self-built AP demo, that boundary shows up as human-only approval for high-risk decisions, with duplicate blocking and audit records around it. That is a demo on synthetic data, not a customer deployment, so the lesson is about control design, not a finished service.

The practical next step is to pick one repeating workflow — invoice approval, customer replies, or lead qualification — and write down the exact point where an acceptance walkthrough happens. Then compare it with your current manual review. If the control is clear and repeatable, bounded automation may fit. If it only works when someone has to hand-hold every step, the workflow is probably not ready. The awkward middle is usually the useful answer.
